2.title: Fullness in Christ: Warnings Against Every Supplement
2.overview:
Now Paul names the danger. Teachers are offering the Colossians a “philosophy” that sounds wise: keep food laws and holy days, practise harsh self-denial, honour angels as mediators, and pursue visions. Its message is “Christ plus”. Paul answers in three steps. First, stay rooted in Christ, as you received him, because all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in him. Second, in him the whole fullness of God dwells bodily, and you are filled in him. You have already been circumcised, buried and raised with him; God made you alive, forgave all your sins, cancelled the record of debt by nailing it to the cross, and disarmed the spiritual powers, leading them in triumph.

Third, therefore let no one judge you over food or holy days, which were shadows of Christ, the substance. Let no one disqualify you with self-made severity, angel worship and visions: such people have let go of the Head, from whom the whole body grows. Rules like “Do not handle, do not taste, do not touch” look wise but have no power to stop the flesh. The cure for sin is not more rules but union with the risen Christ, which chapter 3 unfolds.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Rooted and Built Up in Him
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul wants them to know how hard he is striving for them, for Laodicea and for others who have never met him, so that they may be encouraged, united in love, and rich in understanding of God’s mystery, which is Christ, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden. He says this so that no one deceives them with persuasive talk. Though absent, he rejoices at their good order and firm faith. As they received Christ Jesus as Lord, so they should go on living in him, rooted, built up, established in the faith and overflowing with thanks.
verseByVerse.theology:
All the Treasures of Wisdom Hidden in Christ

Colossians 2:3 — “in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” — is the epistemological foundation of the Reformed tradition’s approach to all knowledge. Cornelius Van Til’s presuppositionalism, Abraham Kuyper’s sphere sovereignty, Francis Schaeffer’s integrated Christian worldview: all are ultimately grounded in this text. All genuine wisdom and knowledge find their coherence and source in Christ. This does not mean that only Christians can know things; it means that all knowledge that is genuinely true is “thinking God’s thoughts after him,” participating (knowingly or not) in the structure of reality that Christ created and sustains. The Christian intellectual task is to follow wisdom wherever it leads, knowing that it leads ultimately to the one in whom all wisdom is hidden.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossian philosophy offered esoteric wisdom that seemed to go beyond what the gospel provided. Paul says: all the wisdom you are seeking is already hidden in Christ. You are not lacking wisdom; you have not been exploring deeply enough the one in whom wisdom dwells. Now: The Christian who turns to secular philosophy, psychology, or spirituality for the wisdom that Christ supposedly cannot provide has accepted the false teachers’ premise. All genuine wisdom, wherever it is found, is a trace of the one in whom all wisdom is hidden. The Christian engages with every source of wisdom while recognizing that Christ is its ultimate source and criterion.

verseByVerse.quote: For I want you to know how great a struggle I have for you and for those at Laodicea and for all who have not seen me face to face,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I want you to know how great a struggle I have for you and for those at Laodicea and for all who have not seen me face to face,

Meaning first. Colossians 2 confronts the false teaching directly, and answers it with Christ. First, Paul explains his struggle in prayer for them: that they may be united in love and come to the full riches of understanding Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. So no one should deceive them with clever arguments; they should keep walking in Christ as they received him (vv. 1–7). Second, he warns against philosophy and human tradition that is not according to Christ. In Christ the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily, and believers are filled in him. They have been spiritually circumcised, buried and raised with him, made alive and forgiven; the record of debt against them was nailed to the cross, and the hostile powers were disarmed and paraded in defeat (vv. 8–15). Third, he draws the conclusion: do not let anyone judge you about food, festivals or Sabbaths, which were shadows of Christ; or disqualify you with angel worship and visions; or bind you with rules like do not handle, do not taste, do not touch. These look wise but have no power against the flesh (vv. 16–23). Christ is enough.

For I want you to know how great a struggle I have for you. Key words. “Struggle” (agōn, contest, conflict), from 1:29. Paul wrestles in prayer and concern for churches he has never visited.

And for those at Laodicea. Key words. Laodicea lay about 10 miles from Colossae, a wealthy banking and textile city (Revelation 3:14–22). Paul wrote them a letter too (4:16).

And for all who have not seen me face to face. Key words. Including Hierapolis and other churches in the valley. Paul’s care reaches beyond those he personally knows.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul’s concern was anxious worry. It was earnest prayer and labour.

In a sentence. Paul wants you to know how hard he is contending for you and for those at Laodicea, and for all who have not met him personally.

On a Tuesday. Struggle in prayer this week for a church you have never visited.
verseByVerse.note: Laodicea lay about 10 miles from Colossae.

verseByVerse.quote: that their hearts may be encouraged, being knit together in love, to reach all the riches of full assurance of understanding and the knowledge of God’s mystery, which is Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
that their hearts may be encouraged, being knit together in love, to reach all the riches of full assurance of understanding and the knowledge of God’s mystery, which is Christ,

That their hearts may be encouraged. Key words. “Encouraged” (parakaleō, strengthened, comforted).

Being knit together in love. Key words. “Knit together” (symbibazō, joined, united, as joints of a body, v. 19). Love unites the church against division by false teaching.

To reach all the riches of full assurance of understanding. Key words. “Full assurance” (plērophoria, complete confidence). Understanding that is certain and settled.

And the knowledge of God’s mystery, which is Christ. Key words. The mystery is not a secret doctrine for initiates, but a person: Christ. To know him is to know God’s mystery. Some manuscripts vary at this point; the ESV reading is well supported.

What it does not mean. It does not mean understanding comes without love. Paul joins them: knit together in love, to reach understanding.

In a sentence. Paul’s goal is that they may be encouraged in heart and united in love, so that they may have the full riches of complete understanding, in order that they may know the mystery of God, namely, Christ,

For worship. Pray for your church to be knit together in love and confident in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.
verseByVerse.commentary:
in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.

In whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. Key words. “Hidden” (apokryphos, stored away, as treasure is kept safe). Not hidden in the sense of inaccessible, but stored up in Christ, to be found by those who seek him. All the treasures: there is no wisdom or knowledge worth having outside Christ. The false teachers offered hidden knowledge beyond Christ; Paul says all of it is already in Christ (1 Corinthians 1:24, 30).

What it does not mean. It does not mean other learning is worthless. All true knowledge belongs to Christ, and leads back to him.

In a sentence. in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.

On a Tuesday. When you seek wisdom for a decision today, seek it in Christ and his word first.

verseByVerse.quote: I say this in order that no one may delude you with plausible arguments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I say this in order that no one may delude you with plausible arguments.

I say this in order that no one may delude you. Key words. “Delude” (paralogizomai, deceive by false reasoning).

With plausible arguments. Key words. “Plausible arguments” (pithanologia, persuasive speech, fine-sounding words). False teaching often sounds attractive and convincing. The defence is to know Christ fully.

What it does not mean. It does not mean persuasion or argument is wrong. It means arguments must be tested by Christ.

In a sentence. Paul tells you this so that no one may deceive you by fine-sounding arguments.

For worship. Ask God to protect you from persuasive error, and to root you in the truth.

verseByVerse.quote: For though I am absent in body, yet I am with you in spirit, rejoicing to see your good order and the firmness of your faith in Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For though I am absent in body, yet I am with you in spirit, rejoicing to see your good order and the firmness of your faith in Christ.

For though I am absent in body, yet I am with you in spirit. Key words. Present in thought, prayer and care (1 Corinthians 5:3).

Rejoicing to see your good order. Key words. “Good order” (taxis, a military term for soldiers in rank). The church was still holding the line.

And the firmness of your faith in Christ. Key words. “Firmness” (stereōma, solid front, a fortified line). They had not yet broken ranks. Paul writes to strengthen them before trouble spreads.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the church was in no danger. It means the danger had not yet overcome them.

In a sentence. For though Paul is absent from you in body, he is present with you in spirit and delights to see how disciplined you are and how firm your faith in Christ is.

On a Tuesday. Hold your place in the ranks. Stand firm in Christ with your church.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, as you received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in him, rooted and built up in him and established in the faith, just as you were taught, abounding in thanksgiving.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore, as you received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in him, rooted and built up in him and established in the faith, just as you were taught, abounding in thanksgiving.

Therefore, as you received Christ Jesus the Lord. Key words. “Received” (paralambanō, the word for receiving tradition). They received not just teaching about Christ but Christ himself, as Lord.

So walk in him. Key words. Continue as you began. The Christian life is lived the same way it starts: by faith in Christ. No new method is needed.

Rooted and built up in him. Key words. Two pictures. Rooted (errizōmenoi, perfect tense: firmly planted once and for all), like a tree. Built up (epoikodomoumenoi, present tense: continually), like a building.

And established in the faith, just as you were taught. Key words. “Established” (bebaioumenoi, confirmed, made firm). In the faith as Epaphras taught it.

Abounding in thanksgiving. Key words. Thankfulness for what one has in Christ protects against seeking something more.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers do not grow. They are continually built up. But always in Christ, not beyond him.

In a sentence. So then, just as you received Christ Jesus as Lord, continue to live your lives in him, rooted and built up in him, strengthened in the faith as you were taught, and overflowing with thankfulness.

For worship. Thank God that you received Christ. Ask him to root you deeper in him today.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul warns them not to be captured by empty, deceptive philosophy rooted in human tradition and the world’s basic principles rather than in Christ. The whole fullness of God lives in Christ bodily, and believers are complete in him, who is head over every power. In him they have received a circumcision not done by hands, the stripping away of the old nature, and in baptism they were buried with him and raised with him through faith in God’s power. God made them alive with Christ, forgave all their sins, cancelled the record of debt that stood against them by nailing it to the cross, and disarmed the hostile powers, exposing them publicly and triumphing over them in Christ.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Cancellation of the Debt and the Disarming of the Powers

Colossians 2:13–15 contains two of the most vivid metaphors for the atonement in the New Testament. First, the legal metaphor: the “record of debt” (cheirographon) that stood against us — the written bond of indebtedness, the document that recorded every sin and violation — has been cancelled, taken out of the way, nailed to the cross. The debt is not merely forgiven; the document is destroyed. Second, the military metaphor: the rulers and authorities who held humanity in their power through guilt and the law’s accusation have been “disarmed” and put to open shame — led in a triumphal procession like conquered enemies behind the victorious general. These two images together show what the cross accomplished: liberation from guilt (the debt cancelled) and liberation from spiritual bondage (the powers defeated).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossian philosophy appealed to the elemental spirits and cosmic powers as real and threatening forces that needed to be placated through ritual observance. Paul says: those powers have been disarmed. They are defeated enemies, paraded in public shame behind the triumphing Christ. You do not placate them; you stand on the victory that has already been won. Now: The Christian who lives in fear of spiritual powers — who approaches life with anxiety about demonic influence, spiritual attack, or cosmic forces working against them — needs to hear this: the powers have been disarmed. Christ has triumphed. The fear of powers that have been publicly defeated is not piety; it is a failure to reckon with the victory of the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: See to it that no one takes you captive by philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elemental spirits of the world, and not according to Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
See to it that no one takes you captive by philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elemental spirits of the world, and not according to Christ.

See to it that no one takes you captive. Key words. “Takes captive” (sylagōgeō, carries off as booty, kidnaps). False teachers are spiritual kidnappers.

By philosophy and empty deceit. Key words. “Philosophy” (philosophia, love of wisdom). Here not philosophy in general, but this particular religious philosophy, which Paul calls empty deceit (one phrase in Greek: philosophy that is empty deceit).

According to human tradition. Key words. Its source is human, not divine (Mark 7:8).

According to the elemental spirits of the world. Key words. “Elemental spirits” (stoicheia) may mean the basic principles of religion or the spirit-powers thought to control the world, as in Galatians 4:3, 9. The false teaching was earth-bound, either elementary rules or dealings with spiritual powers.

And not according to Christ. Key words. The decisive test: is it according to Christ?

Where Christians differ: should Christians study philosophy? Some take this verse to forbid all philosophy. Verdict: Paul condemns philosophy that is empty deceit, rooted in human tradition and not according to Christ. Christians may study philosophy, and many great Christian thinkers have, but must bring every thought captive to Christ (2 Corinthians 10:5) and judge all systems by Scripture. Philosophy is a good servant and a bad master.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians should be anti-intellectual. Christ contains all treasures of wisdom (v. 3).

In a sentence. See to it that no one takes you captive through hollow and deceptive philosophy, which depends on human tradition and the elemental spiritual forces of this world rather than on Christ.

On a Tuesday. Test the ideas you meet today, in books, news and conversation: are they according to Christ?
verseByVerse.note: “Elemental spirits” may mean the basic principles of religion or the spiritual powers people believed ruled the world.

verseByVerse.quote: For in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily,

For in him the whole fullness of deity. Key words. “Deity” (theotēs, Godhead, the divine nature itself, not just divine qualities). The whole of it, not a portion.

Dwells bodily. Key words. “Dwells” (present tense: continues to dwell, permanently). “Bodily” (sōmatikōs): in a human body. The incarnate Christ, now risen, is fully God in human flesh. The strongest statement in Scripture of the full deity of the incarnate Christ.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the divine nature was turned into flesh. It means the eternal Son, fully God, took human nature, so that God dwells fully in the man Christ Jesus.

In a sentence. For in Christ all the fullness of the Deity lives in bodily form,

For worship. Worship Jesus Christ, fully God in a human body, now and forever.

verseByVerse.quote: and you have been filled in him, who is the head of all rule and authority.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and you have been filled in him, who is the head of all rule and authority.

And you have been filled in him. Key words. “Filled” (peplērōmenoi, perfect tense: brought to fullness, and remain so). Since God’s fullness is in Christ, and believers are in Christ, they lack nothing. The false teachers said believers needed more for completeness. Paul says: you are already complete in Christ.

Who is the head of all rule and authority. Key words. Christ rules over all spiritual powers. Why seek help from angels or spirits, when you are joined to their Lord?

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers have nothing more to grow into. They grow in experiencing what they already have.

In a sentence. and in Christ you have been brought to fullness. He is the head over every power and authority.

On a Tuesday. You are complete in Christ. Stop looking for something extra to make you whole.

verseByVerse.quote: In him also you were circumcised with a circumcision made without hands, by putting off the body of the flesh, by the circumcision of Christ, having been buried with him in baptism, in which you were also raised with him through faith in the powerful working of God, who raised him from the dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In him also you were circumcised with a circumcision made without hands, by putting off the body of the flesh, by the circumcision of Christ, having been buried with him in baptism, in which you were also raised with him through faith in the powerful working of God, who raised him from the dead.

In him also you were circumcised with a circumcision made without hands. Key words. Spiritual circumcision: the cutting away of the sinful nature, which the Old Testament promised (Deuteronomy 30:6; Jeremiah 4:4). Not done by human hands but by God. So the Colossians need no physical circumcision.

By putting off the body of the flesh. Key words. The old sinful nature stripped off, like a garment (3:9).

By the circumcision of Christ. Key words. Either the circumcision Christ performs, or Christ’s own “circumcision,” his death, in which his body was cut off. Either way, union with Christ achieves what circumcision pointed to.

Having been buried with him in baptism. Key words. Baptism signifies union with Christ in his death and burial (Romans 6:3–4). Going under the water pictures burial.

In which you were also raised with him through faith in the powerful working of God. Key words. And rising pictures resurrection with Christ. Through faith: the union is received by faith in God’s power that raised Jesus.

Who raised him from the dead. Key words. The same power raises believers to new life.

Where Christians differ: does baptism replace circumcision? Paedobaptists argue from this verse that baptism is the new covenant sign replacing circumcision, and so, as circumcision was given to infants, baptism should be too. Verdict: The circumcision Paul links with baptism is the spiritual circumcision of the heart made without hands, and the raising happens “through faith.” What replaces physical circumcision is regeneration, and baptism signifies that inward reality, which is received by faith. So the sign belongs to those who show the reality: believers. The app holds believer’s baptism, while warmly respecting paedobaptist brothers and sisters who read the covenant signs differently.

What it does not mean. It does not mean baptism itself saves. It signifies union with Christ, received by faith.

In a sentence. In him you were also circumcised with a circumcision not performed by human hands. Your whole self ruled by the flesh was put off when you were circumcised by Christ, having been buried with him in baptism, in which you were also raised with him through your faith in the working of God, who raised him from the dead.

For worship. Thank God that you were buried and raised with Christ. Live as one raised to new life.

verseByVerse.quote: And you, who were dead in your trespasses and the uncircumcision of your flesh, God made alive together with him, having forgiven us all our trespasses, by canceling the record of debt that stood against us with its legal demands. This he set aside, nailing it to the cross.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And you, who were dead in your trespasses and the uncircumcision of your flesh, God made alive together with him, having forgiven us all our trespasses, by canceling the record of debt that stood against us with its legal demands. This he set aside, nailing it to the cross.

And you, who were dead in your trespasses. Key words. Spiritually dead, unable to respond to God (Ephesians 2:1, 5).

And the uncircumcision of your flesh. Key words. Outside God’s covenant, and unchanged at heart.

God made alive together with him. Key words. Regeneration: God gave new life, in union with the risen Christ. The dead cannot make themselves alive.

Having forgiven us all our trespasses. Key words. “Forgiven” (charizomai, freely, graciously). All: past, present, future. Notice Paul shifts from “you” to “us”: he includes himself.

By canceling the record of debt that stood against us with its legal demands. Key words. The “record of debt” (cheirographon) was a handwritten certificate of debt signed by the debtor, an IOU. Our debt to God’s law, with its demands, stood against us. “Cancelling” (exaleiphō, wiping out, as writing was washed off papyrus).

This he set aside, nailing it to the cross. Key words. Over a crucified criminal, the charge was nailed (John 19:19). Over Jesus, God nailed our debt. The charge against us was paid in full by his death. This is penal substitution.

What it does not mean. It does not mean God ignored the debt. It was paid by Christ.

In a sentence. When you were dead in your sins and in the uncircumcision of your flesh, God made you alive with Christ. He forgave us all our sins, having cancelled the charge of our legal indebtedness, which stood against us and condemned us; he has taken it away, nailing it to the cross.

On a Tuesday. Your debt is cancelled. When guilt accuses you today, point to the cross.
verseByVerse.note: The “record of debt” was a handwritten certificate of debt signed by the debtor; the charge against a crucified man was nailed above him.

verseByVerse.quote: He disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him.

He disarmed the rulers and authorities. Key words. “Disarmed” (apekdyomai, stripped, as defeated soldiers were stripped of weapons and armour). The spiritual powers of evil lost their power to accuse and enslave.

And put them to open shame. Key words. Made a public spectacle of them.

By triumphing over them in him. Key words. A Roman general celebrated victory by parading his captives through the streets in a triumph. At the cross, Christ led the defeated powers in his victory parade. What looked like Christ’s defeat was his triumph. “In him” (or “in it,” the cross).

What it does not mean. It does not mean evil powers no longer exist or act. They are defeated but not yet destroyed; their final end comes at Christ’s return (Revelation 20:10).

In a sentence. And having disarmed the powers and authorities, he made a public spectacle of them, triumphing over them by the cross.

For worship. The powers that frighten you are defeated foes. Praise Christ for his triumph at the cross.
verseByVerse.note: A Roman general celebrated victory by parading his captives through the streets.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: So no one should judge them over food and drink, festivals, new moons or sabbaths; these were shadows of what was to come, and the reality is Christ. They must not let anyone disqualify them who insists on self-abasement, the worship of angels and claims of visions, puffed up by an unspiritual mind and not holding on to Christ the head, from whom the whole body grows. Since they died with Christ to the world’s basic principles, why submit to rules like “do not handle, do not taste”? Such regulations, based on human teaching, look wise with their strict religion and harsh treatment of the body, but they are powerless to restrain the flesh.
verseByVerse.theology:
Shadow and Substance: The Old Covenant as Anticipation

Paul’s description of the Mosaic observances as “a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ” (v. 17) is the hermeneutical principle underlying all Reformed typological interpretation of the Old Testament. The ceremonial law — the festivals, the sabbaths, the food laws, the sacrificial system — was genuinely given by God and genuinely pointed forward to the reality that was coming. But it was always a shadow, not the substance; always anticipation, not fulfilment. The substance arrived in Christ. To return to the shadow when the substance is present is not faithfulness to the law; it is a failure to read what the law was always saying.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossian teachers were using Jewish observances as part of their syncretic system, insisting that the Colossians needed to keep certain days and food laws and festivals. Paul says: these were shadows pointing to Christ; Christ has come. Now: The same principle applies to any Christian movement that makes Old Testament ceremonial practices the standard of Christian spirituality. The principles of justice, love, and holiness that the ceremonial law expressed are fulfilled in Christ and applied by the Spirit. The specific ceremonies have been fulfilled in him who was their substance all along.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore let no one pass judgment on you in questions of food and drink, or with regard to a festival or a new moon or a Sabbath.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore let no one pass judgment on you in questions of food and drink, or with regard to a festival or a new moon or a Sabbath.

Therefore let no one pass judgment on you. Key words. Because of Christ’s complete work, believers are free. Do not let anyone condemn you or set conditions.

In questions of food and drink. Key words. The food laws of Moses, and perhaps ascetic rules (v. 21).

Or with regard to a festival or a new moon or a Sabbath. Key words. The three kinds of holy days in Israel’s calendar: annual festivals, monthly new moons, weekly Sabbaths (1 Chronicles 23:31; Hosea 2:11). All three are included.

Where Christians differ: the Sabbath. Some say Christians must keep the seventh-day Sabbath; others that the fourth commandment transfers fully to Sunday with all its strictness. Verdict: Paul includes the Sabbath among the shadows fulfilled in Christ (v. 17). Christians are not bound by the Mosaic Sabbath law, and no one may judge them for not keeping it. Christ is our rest (Matthew 11:28; Hebrews 4:9–10). The Lord’s Day, the day of resurrection, is the day the church gathers for worship (Acts 20:7; Revelation 1:10): a privilege and a gift, and a wise pattern of rest, not a legal burden.

What it does not mean. It does not mean rest and worship are unimportant. It means they are not means of righteousness.

In a sentence. Therefore do not let anyone judge you by what you eat or drink, or with regard to a religious festival, a New Moon celebration or a Sabbath day.

On a Tuesday. Do not let anyone burden your conscience with rules Christ has fulfilled. Rest in him.

verseByVerse.quote: These are a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These are a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ.

These are a shadow of the things to come. Key words. “Shadow” (skia): an outline cast by an object. The food laws and holy days pointed forward to Christ (Hebrews 8:5; 10:1).

But the substance belongs to Christ. Key words. “Substance” (sōma, body). The reality that cast the shadow is Christ. Once the body has arrived, why cling to its shadow?

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Old Testament is worthless. Shadows are real and point to the real thing. Studying them helps us see Christ.

In a sentence. These are a shadow of the things that were to come; the reality, however, is found in Christ.

For worship. Thank God that you have the substance, Christ himself, not only the shadows.

verseByVerse.quote: Let no one disqualify you, insisting on asceticism and worship of angels, going on in detail about visions, puffed up without reason by his sensuous mind,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let no one disqualify you, insisting on asceticism and worship of angels, going on in detail about visions, puffed up without reason by his sensuous mind,

Let no one disqualify you. Key words. “Disqualify” (katabrabeuō, rule against, like an umpire denying a prize). Do not let anyone tell you that you do not qualify for the prize because you lack their experiences.

Insisting on asceticism. Key words. “Asceticism” (tapeinophrosynē, literally humility, but here false humility: harsh self-denial, fasting as a spiritual technique).

And worship of angels. Key words. Either worshipping angels, or joining in the worship angels offer, in visionary experiences. The false teaching seems to have mixed Jewish rules, strict self-denial and mystical experiences of the angelic world.

Going on in detail about visions. Key words. “Going on in detail” (embateuō, entering into, a word used in the mystery religions for initiates entering the sanctuary). They took their stand on visions they claimed to have seen.

Puffed up without reason by his sensuous mind. Key words. Literally, the mind of his flesh. For all their spirituality, their minds were fleshly and proud.

Where Christians differ: praying to angels and saints. Some traditions encourage prayer to angels or departed saints for help and intercession. Verdict: Paul warns against worship of angels, and Scripture forbids worshipping any creature (Revelation 19:10; 22:8–9). There is one mediator between God and man, Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5), and he always lives to intercede for us (Hebrews 7:25). Believers pray to God through Christ alone.

What it does not mean. It does not mean fasting is wrong. Jesus expected his followers to fast (Matthew 6:16). It means fasting as a technique for spiritual superiority is wrong.

In a sentence. Do not let anyone who delights in false humility and the worship of angels disqualify you. Such a person also goes into great detail about what they have seen; they are puffed up with idle notions by their unspiritual mind.

On a Tuesday. Do not let anyone make you feel second-class for lacking their spiritual experiences. You have Christ.
verseByVerse.note: The false teaching seems to have mixed Jewish rules, strict self-denial and fascination with angels and visions.

verseByVerse.quote: and not holding fast to the Head, from whom the whole body, nourished and knit together through its joints and ligaments, grows with a growth that is from God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and not holding fast to the Head, from whom the whole body, nourished and knit together through its joints and ligaments, grows with a growth that is from God.

And not holding fast to the Head. Key words. The root problem of the false teachers: they had let go of Christ. All true spirituality holds on to him.

From whom the whole body. Key words. The church, the body of Christ (1:18).

Nourished and knit together through its joints and ligaments. Key words. Medical language. Christ, the head, supplies life to the body through the connections between its members. Believers grow through their relationships with one another in the church (Ephesians 4:15–16).

Grows with a growth that is from God. Key words. True growth comes from God, through Christ, not through rules or visions.

What it does not mean. It does not mean growth happens without effort. It means its source is God.

In a sentence. They have lost connection with the head, from whom the whole body, supported and held together by its ligaments and sinews, grows as God causes it to grow.

For worship. Hold fast to Christ the head today. And thank God for the believers through whom he nourishes you.

verseByVerse.quote: If with Christ you died to the elemental spirits of the world, why, as if you were still alive in the world, do you submit to regulations— “Do not handle, Do not taste, Do not touch” (referring to things that all perish as they are used)—according to human precepts and teachings? These have indeed an appearance of wisdom in promoting self-made religion and asceticism and severity to the body, but they are of no value in stopping the indulgence of the flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If with Christ you died to the elemental spirits of the world, why, as if you were still alive in the world, do you submit to regulations—“Do not handle, Do not taste, Do not touch” (referring to things that all perish as they are used)—according to human precepts and teachings? These have indeed an appearance of wisdom in promoting self-made religion and asceticism and severity to the body, but they are of no value in stopping the indulgence of the flesh.

If with Christ you died to the elemental spirits of the world. Key words. Since you died with Christ, you are no longer under that old order of rules and powers.

Why, as if you were still alive in the world, do you submit to regulations. Key words. “Submit to regulations” (dogmatizō, be subjected to decrees).

“Do not handle, Do not taste, Do not touch.” Key words. The slogans of the false teachers. Rules multiplying, each stricter than the last.

(Referring to things that all perish as they are used). Key words. Food and drink are used up and gone. They cannot touch the soul (Mark 7:18–19).

According to human precepts and teachings? Key words. From Isaiah 29:13, quoted by Jesus (Mark 7:7). Human rules, not God’s commands.

These have indeed an appearance of wisdom. Key words. They look impressive and spiritual.

In promoting self-made religion. Key words. “Self-made religion” (ethelothrēskia, will-worship, worship invented by one’s own will).

And asceticism and severity to the body. Key words. Harsh treatment of the body as a path to holiness.

But they are of no value in stopping the indulgence of the flesh. Key words. The devastating verdict. Rules cannot change the heart. They may restrain behaviour outwardly, but they feed pride and leave sinful desires untouched. Only union with Christ, dead and risen, defeats the flesh (3:1–5).

Where Christians differ: rules for holiness. Many churches add rules beyond Scripture: no alcohol, no dancing, strict dress codes, as tests of holiness. Verdict: Christians may make wise personal choices and churches may give wise counsel, but when human rules are made a test of spirituality or bound on others’ consciences, they become self-made religion. God alone is Lord of the conscience, and nothing is to be required beyond his word (Westminster 20.2). The power to defeat sin is found in Christ, not in rules.

What it does not mean. It does not mean self-discipline is useless. Paul disciplined his body (1 Corinthians 9:27). It means discipline cannot replace Christ.

In a sentence. Since you died with Christ to the elemental spiritual forces of this world, why, as though you still belonged to the world, do you submit to its rules: “Do not handle! Do not taste! Do not touch!”? These rules, which have to do with things that are all destined to perish with use, are based on merely human commands and teachings. Such regulations indeed have an appearance of wisdom, with their self-imposed worship, their false humility and their harsh treatment of the body, but they lack any value in restraining sensual indulgence.

For worship. If you have been fighting sin with rules alone, turn to Christ. Ask him to change your heart.

2.text: <sup>1</sup>For I want you to know how great a struggle I have for you and for those at Laodicea and for all who have not seen me face to face,<sup>2</sup>that their hearts may be encouraged, being knit together in love, to reach all the riches of full assurance of understanding and the knowledge of God’s mystery, which is Christ,<sup>3</sup>in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.<sup>4</sup>I say this in order that no one may delude you with plausible arguments.<sup>5</sup>For though I am absent in body, yet I am with you in spirit, rejoicing to see your good order and the firmness of your faith in Christ.<sup>6</sup>Therefore, as you received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in him,<sup>7</sup>rooted and built up in him and established in the faith, just as you were taught, abounding in thanksgiving.<sup>8</sup>See to it that no one takes you captive by philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elemental spirits of the world, and not according to Christ.<sup>9</sup>For in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily,<sup>10</sup>and you have been filled in him, who is the head of all rule and authority.<sup>11</sup>In him also you were circumcised with a circumcision made without hands, by putting off the body of the flesh, by the circumcision of Christ,<sup>12</sup>having been buried with him in baptism, in which you were also raised with him through faith in the powerful working of God, who raised him from the dead.<sup>13</sup>And you, who were dead in your trespasses and the uncircumcision of your flesh, God made alive together with him, having forgiven us all our trespasses,<sup>14</sup>by canceling the record of debt that stood against us with its legal demands. This he set aside, nailing it to the cross.<sup>15</sup>He disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him.<sup>16</sup>Therefore let no one pass judgment on you in questions of food and drink, or with regard to a festival or a new moon or a Sabbath.<sup>17</sup>These are a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ.<sup>18</sup>Let no one disqualify you, insisting on asceticism and worship of angels, going on in detail about visions, puffed up without reason by his sensuous mind,<sup>19</sup>and not holding fast to the Head, from whom the whole body, nourished and knit together through its joints and ligaments, grows with a growth that is from God.<sup>20</sup>If with Christ you died to the elemental spirits of the world, why, as if you were still alive in the world, do you submit to regulations—<sup>21</sup>“Do not handle, Do not taste, Do not touch”<sup>22</sup>(referring to things that all perish as they are used)—according to human precepts and teachings?<sup>23</sup>These have indeed an appearance of wisdom in promoting self-made religion and asceticism and severity to the body, but they are of no value in stopping the indulgence of the flesh.

3.title: Set Your Minds on Things Above: The Old and the New
3.overview:
Chapter 2 showed that rules cannot defeat sin. Chapter 3 gives the real cure: union with the risen Christ. Since you have been raised with him, set your heart and mind on things above, where Christ reigns; your life is hidden with him and will appear with him in glory. Therefore put to death the old sins (sexual immorality, greed, which is idolatry) and strip off anger, malice, slander and lies, because you have already put off the old self and put on the new, which God is renewing in his image. In this new humanity race, religion, culture and class no longer divide: Christ is all, and in all.

Instead, as God’s chosen and beloved people, put on compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, patience and forgiveness, and above all love. Let Christ’s peace rule, let his word dwell in you richly through teaching and song, and do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks. Finally Christ’s lordship enters the home: wives and husbands, children and fathers, slaves and masters, each with a duty, and those with power given the harder command.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Set Your Minds on Things Above
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul draws the consequence of union with Christ. Because believers have already been raised with him, their ambitions and thinking should be directed to heaven, where Christ reigns, rather than to the earthly concerns that once ruled them. Their old life has ended and their real life is now kept safe with Christ in God, out of sight for the moment. When Christ appears, that hidden life will be revealed, and they will share his glory.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Hidden Life and the Security of the Believer in Christ

Colossians 3:3 — “your life is hidden with Christ in God” — is one of the New Testament’s most comprehensive statements of the security of the believer. The life of the Christian is not exposed to the attacks of the world, the flesh, or the devil in any ultimate sense; it is hidden, concealed, kept safe in the most secure location possible: with Christ, in God. Reformed theology has always grounded assurance of salvation not in the believer’s performance but in the security of their position: in Christ, kept by God. This is why the Christian can face the world’s hostility and the flesh’s internal rebellion without ultimate despair; the life that matters is in a place nothing can reach.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossians were being told that their spiritual security depended on correct navigation of the angelic hierarchy, proper observance of festivals and food laws, and achievement of special spiritual states. Paul says: your life is hidden with Christ in God. There is no spiritual power that can reach it; no ritual failure that can revoke it; no ignorance of esoteric knowledge that can diminish it. Now: The Christian whose sense of security rises and falls with their spiritual performance — who feels secure on days of devotional discipline and insecure on days of failure — needs to hear this: your life is hidden. It is not at risk. It is kept by the one whose power infinitely exceeds every force that would threaten it.

verseByVerse.quote: If then you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If then you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God.

Meaning first. Colossians 3 shows the true way to holiness, after chapter 2 rejected the false way of rules. The power for a holy life is union with Christ: believers have died and been raised with him, their life is hidden with him in God, and they will appear with him in glory. So set your minds on things above (vv. 1–4). Then put to death what is earthly: sexual sin, impurity, evil desire and greed, which is idolatry; and put away anger, malice, slander, filthy talk and lying. You have taken off the old self and put on the new, being renewed in the image of your Creator, in a community where Christ is all and in all (vv. 5–11). Put on, as God’s chosen and beloved people, compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness and patience; forgive as the Lord forgave you; and above all put on love. Let Christ’s peace rule, let his word dwell richly in you as you teach and sing, and do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus with thanks (vv. 12–17). Finally, Paul shows what this looks like in the household: wives and husbands, children and fathers, slaves and masters, all living as those who serve the Lord Christ (3:18–4:1).

If then you have been raised with Christ. Key words. “If” here means since. Believers were raised with Christ in union with him (2:12). This is a fact, not a goal.

Seek the things that are above. Key words. “Seek” (zēteō, aim at, pursue, present tense: keep seeking). Things above: the realm where Christ reigns, heavenly realities and values.

Where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God. Key words. The place of supreme honour and authority (Psalm 110:1). Our head is there, so our hearts should be there (Matthew 6:21).

What it does not mean. It does not mean ignoring earthly duties. The rest of the chapter deals with home and work. It means seeing them from heaven’s point of view.

In a sentence. Since, then, you have been raised with Christ, set your hearts on things above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God.

On a Tuesday. Before your day fills with earthly concerns, lift your heart to Christ seated in heaven.

verseByVerse.quote: Set your minds on things that are above, not on things that are on earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Set your minds on things that are above, not on things that are on earth.

Set your minds on things that are above. Key words. “Set your minds” (phroneō, think about, be intent on). Seeking (v. 1) involves the will; setting the mind involves thought. Think heavenly thoughts: about Christ, his glory, his kingdom, his return.

Not on things that are on earth. Key words. Not the earthly things of 2:21–22 (rules about food) or 3:5 (sinful desires). Not that the earth is evil, but that earthly things must not be our mind’s home.

What it does not mean. It does not mean being so heavenly minded as to be no earthly good. Heavenly minded people make the best earthly servants.

In a sentence. Set your minds on things above, not on earthly things.

For worship. Spend a few minutes today thinking about Christ in glory.

verseByVerse.quote: For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.

For you have died. Key words. Past tense: with Christ, to sin, the world and the old life (2:20; Romans 6:2–7).

And your life is hidden with Christ in God. Key words. “Hidden” (kryptō, perfect tense: has been hidden and remains so). Your true life is safe with Christ, kept in God, like treasure in a vault. No one can reach it to destroy it. It is also hidden in the sense of not yet visible to the world.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers have no life now. It means their real life is secure in Christ.

In a sentence. For you died, and your life is now hidden with Christ in God.

On a Tuesday. Your life is hidden with Christ. Whatever happens today, it is safe.

verseByVerse.quote: When Christ who is your life appears, then you also will appear with him in glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Christ who is your life appears, then you also will appear with him in glory.

When Christ who is your life appears. Key words. Christ is your life: not just the giver, but the substance of it (Philippians 1:21; Galatians 2:20). “Appears” (phaneroō, is revealed): his return in glory.

Then you also will appear with him in glory. Key words. What is now hidden will be revealed. Believers will share Christ’s glory publicly (Romans 8:18–19; 1 John 3:2).

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers will become divine. They will share his glory as glorified humans.

In a sentence. When Christ, who is your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory.

For worship. Christ is your life. Thank him that one day you will appear with him in glory.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–11 — Put to Death, Put Off
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: So they must put to death everything in them that belongs to the earth: sexual immorality, impurity, lust, evil desire and greed, which is idolatry. These bring God’s wrath, and they once lived that way. Now they must also get rid of anger, rage, malice, slander and filthy talk, and stop lying to one another, since they have taken off the old self and put on the new, which is being renewed in knowledge after its Creator’s image. In that new humanity the old divisions of race, religion, culture and class no longer count; Christ is all, and in all.
verseByVerse.theology:
Mortification: Putting to Death What Christ Has Already Condemned

John Owen’s great treatise Of the Mortification of Sin in Believers is the most sustained Reformed treatment of what Paul commands in Colossians 3:5. Owen’s central principle — “be killing sin, or it will be killing you” — reflects Paul’s logic exactly. The mortification Paul calls for is not the ascetic self-punishment that the Colossian false teachers practiced and Paul has just condemned (2:23); it is the Spirit-enabled application of the cross to specific sinful desires, the practical reckoning with what Christ accomplished: these desires belong to the old self that died in Christ; by the Spirit I put them to death.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossians were being offered an ascetic program that promised to deal with the flesh by external denial. Paul says: that program has no value in stopping the flesh’s indulgence (2:23). The real program is mortification — not external prohibition but the internal death-dealing of the Spirit to specific desires. The difference is not severity (asceticism can be more severe than mortification) but source: mortification flows from union with the crucified Christ. Now: The Christian who is fighting sin through willpower and self-discipline alone is using the wrong weapons. Mortification is spiritual warfare: the application of Christ’s death to specific sin patterns, in prayer, by the Spirit, in the community of faith. The fight is real; the weapon is the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: Put to death therefore what is earthly in you: sexual immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire, and covetousness, which is idolatry.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Put to death therefore what is earthly in you: sexual immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire, and covetousness, which is idolatry.

Put to death therefore. Key words. “Put to death” (nekroō, kill, mortify). Therefore: because you died and were raised with Christ. Become what you are. Kill sin, do not merely manage it (Romans 8:13). John Owen’s famous saying: be killing sin or it will be killing you.

What is earthly in you. Key words. Literally your members on the earth: the sinful desires still at work in your body.

Sexual immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire. Key words. A progression from outward act to inner desire. Sexual immorality (porneia), impurity (akatharsia), passion (pathos, uncontrolled lust), evil desire (epithymia kakē).

And covetousness, which is idolatry. Key words. Covetousness (pleonexia, greed, always wanting more). Why idolatry? Because greed makes something other than God the object of our desire and trust (Matthew 6:24; Ephesians 5:5). The respectable sin is named as idolatry.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the body is evil. It means sinful desires must be killed.

In a sentence. Put to death, therefore, whatever belongs to your earthly nature: sexual immorality, impurity, lust, evil desires and greed, which is idolatry.

On a Tuesday. Name one earthly desire that is ruling you. Ask Christ for power to put it to death today.

verseByVerse.quote: On account of these the wrath of God is coming.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On account of these the wrath of God is coming.

On account of these the wrath of God is coming. Key words. God’s just anger against sin is not a myth. It is coming at the judgement (Romans 1:18; 2:5; Ephesians 5:6). Some manuscripts add “upon the sons of disobedience.” Believers are rescued from it by Christ (1 Thessalonians 1:10), but they must not live in the sins that bring it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers will face God’s wrath. Christ bore it for them. It means sin is deadly serious.

In a sentence. Because of these, the wrath of God is coming.

For worship. Thank Christ that he bore God’s wrath for you. Let that make you hate the sins that caused it.

verseByVerse.quote: In these you too once walked, when you were living in them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In these you too once walked, when you were living in them.

In these you too once walked, when you were living in them. Key words. The Colossians’ past. They lived in these sins before Christ. Once: but no longer. A reminder of grace, and a call to leave the past behind.

What it does not mean. It does not mean believers never fall into these sins. It means these no longer define their life.

In a sentence. You used to walk in these ways, in the life you once lived.

On a Tuesday. Remember what you once were. Thank God that it is in the past.

verseByVerse.quote: But now you must put them all away: anger, wrath, malice, slander, and obscene talk from your mouth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But now you must put them all away: anger, wrath, malice, slander, and obscene talk from your mouth.

But now you must put them all away. Key words. “Put away” (apotithēmi, take off, as dirty clothes).

Anger, wrath. Key words. Anger (orgē, settled, smouldering hostility) and wrath (thymos, outbursts of rage).

Malice. Key words. “Malice” (kakia, ill will, wishing harm).

Slander, and obscene talk from your mouth. Key words. Slander (blasphēmia, speaking evil of others). Obscene talk (aischrologia, filthy, abusive language). Sins of the tongue. The first list (v. 5) was sexual and greedy; this one is relational and verbal. Respectable church members can be guilty of these.

What it does not mean. It does not mean all anger is sin. Jesus was angry at sin (Mark 3:5). It means sinful, selfish anger must go (Ephesians 4:26).

In a sentence. But now you must also rid yourselves of all such things as these: anger, rage, malice, slander and filthy language from your lips.

For worship. Ask God to cleanse your heart of anger and your mouth of harsh words.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not lie to one another, seeing that you have put off the old self with its practices and have put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not lie to one another, seeing that you have put off the old self with its practices and have put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator.

Do not lie to one another. Key words. Truthfulness is essential to Christian community (Ephesians 4:25).

Seeing that you have put off the old self with its practices. Key words. “Old self” (literally old man): the person you were in Adam, before Christ. Put off at conversion, like old clothes.

And have put on the new self. Key words. The new person in Christ. Both are past tense: done at conversion. Now live out what has happened.

Which is being renewed in knowledge. Key words. Present tense: continually being made new. The new self grows.

After the image of its creator. Key words. Restored to the image of God, lost in the fall (Genesis 1:26–27; Ephesians 4:24), which is the image of Christ (1:15; Romans 8:29). Salvation is new creation.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the old self is gone in every respect. The flesh still fights (Galatians 5:17). But the believer’s identity is the new self.

In a sentence. Do not lie to each other, since you have taken off your old self with its practices and have put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge in the image of its Creator.

On a Tuesday. You have put on the new self. Dress the part today: speak truthfully.

verseByVerse.quote: Here there is not Greek and Jew, circumcised and uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave, free; but Christ is all, and in all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here there is not Greek and Jew, circumcised and uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave, free; but Christ is all, and in all.

Here there is not Greek and Jew, circumcised and uncircumcised. Key words. Here: in the new humanity. Ethnic and religious divisions lose their power.

Barbarian, Scythian. Key words. Barbarians: non-Greeks, thought uncivilised. Scythians, from north of the Black Sea, were thought of as the most savage of all. Even they are welcome as equals in Christ.

Slave, free. Key words. Social class does not count before God.

But Christ is all, and in all. Key words. Christ is everything: all that matters. And he is in all believers, uniting them. The same Christ in the Scythian and the Jew.

What it does not mean. It does not mean cultural differences disappear. It means they no longer divide or rank.

In a sentence. Here there is no Gentile or Jew, circumcised or uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave or free, but Christ is all, and is in all.

For worship. Thank God for believers from every nation and class. Christ is in them all.
verseByVerse.note: Scythians, from north of the Black Sea, were thought of as the most uncivilised of barbarians.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: As God’s chosen people, holy and loved, they are to clothe themselves with compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness and patience, bearing with and forgiving one another as the Lord forgave them, and above all with love, which binds everything together. Christ’s peace is to rule in their hearts, and they should be thankful. The word of Christ is to dwell richly among them as they teach and admonish one another and sing to God with gratitude. Whatever they do, in word or deed, they are to do it in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to the Father through him.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Virtues of the New Self as the Character of Christ

The list of virtues in Colossians 3:12–15 is nothing less than a portrait of Christ himself: compassionate, kind, humble, meek, patient, forgiving, loving, peaceful. Reformed theology understands sanctification as progressive conformity to the image of Christ (Rom 8:29); the virtues Paul commands here are the specific contours of that image. They are not generated by the believer through moral effort; they are produced by the Spirit as the fruit of genuine union with Christ (compare the fruit of the Spirit in Galatians 5:22–23). The community that puts on these virtues is the community that is becoming what it already is in Christ: holy and beloved.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Colossian community, like every early Christian community, was a mixture of people from very different backgrounds — Jewish, Greek, slave, free — with very different habits of relating and conflicting. The virtues Paul commands were counter-cultural in every direction: humility was scorned by Graeco-Roman aristocratic culture; forgiveness was a novelty in a world organized around honour and revenge. Now: The church remains the most diverse social reality in the world, and the virtues Paul commands remain equally counter-cultural. The church that is genuinely putting on compassion, kindness, humility, and forbearance will look radically different from any other community the world contains, because these virtues are the character of the one who was raised for us.

verseByVerse.quote: Put on then, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, compassionate hearts, kindness, humility, meekness, and patience, bearing with one another and, if one has a complaint against another, forgiving each other; as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive. And above all these put on love, which binds everything together in perfect harmony.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Put on then, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, compassionate hearts, kindness, humility, meekness, and patience, bearing with one another and, if one has a complaint against another, forgiving each other; as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive. And above all these put on love, which binds everything together in perfect harmony.

Put on then, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved. Key words. Three titles that once belonged to Israel. Chosen (eklektoi): elected by God. Holy: set apart. Beloved: loved by God. Our identity comes first, then the commands. Because you are chosen and loved, put on these qualities.

Compassionate hearts, kindness, humility, meekness, and patience. Key words. Five virtues, all describing Christ. Compassion (literally bowels of mercy, deep feeling for others). Kindness. Humility (lowliness of mind). Meekness (gentleness, strength under control). Patience (long-suffering).

Bearing with one another. Key words. Putting up with each other’s faults and quirks.

And, if one has a complaint against another, forgiving each other. Key words. “Forgiving” (charizomai, graciously pardoning). When real wrongs happen, forgive.

As the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive. Key words. The measure and motive. Christ forgave us freely, fully, at great cost. So we forgive (Matthew 18:21–35; Ephesians 4:32).

And above all these put on love. Key words. Love is the outer garment, over all the others.

Which binds everything together in perfect harmony. Key words. “Binds” (syndesmos, bond, belt, ligament). Love holds all the virtues together, and holds the church together.

What it does not mean. It does not mean ignoring serious sin. Forgiveness does not always remove consequences or immediately restore trust. But it releases the debt.

In a sentence. Therefore, as God’s chosen people, holy and dearly loved, clothe yourselves with compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness and patience. Bear with each other and forgive one another if any of you has a grievance against someone. Forgive as the Lord forgave you. And over all these virtues put on love, which binds them all together in perfect unity.

On a Tuesday. Who do you need to forgive? Remember how the Lord forgave you, and forgive them today.

verseByVerse.quote: And let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts, to which indeed you were called in one body. And be thankful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts, to which indeed you were called in one body. And be thankful.

And let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts. Key words. “Rule” (brabeuō, act as umpire, decide). Christ’s peace should be the referee in your heart and in the church, settling disputes and decisions.

To which indeed you were called in one body. Key words. God called believers into one body, the church. Peace is the church’s calling.

And be thankful. Key words. “Thankful” (eucharistos). Thankfulness is the third time in this letter (1:12; 2:7). Grateful people make peace; grumbling people break it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean a feeling of peace always shows God’s will. It means Christ’s peace should govern relationships and decisions.

In a sentence. Let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts, since as members of one body you were called to peace. And be thankful.

For worship. Ask Christ’s peace to rule your heart today. Then give thanks.

verseByVerse.quote: Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly, teaching and admonishing one another in all wisdom, singing psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, with thankfulness in your hearts to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly, teaching and admonishing one another in all wisdom, singing psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, with thankfulness in your hearts to God.

Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly. Key words. The word of Christ: the message about Christ, and his own words. “Dwell” (enoikeō, live in, make its home). Richly: abundantly. Not a visitor but a resident. “In you” is plural: among you as a church.

Teaching and admonishing one another in all wisdom. Key words. All believers teach and counsel one another from the word (Romans 15:14).

Singing psalms and hymns and spiritual songs. Key words. Psalms: the Old Testament Psalms. Hymns: songs of praise. Spiritual songs: songs given by the Spirit. Singing is one way the word dwells in the church: we teach one another as we sing.

With thankfulness in your hearts to God. Key words. Literally, with grace, or with gratitude. Singing from the heart, not just the lips.

Where Christians differ: what should churches sing? Some Reformed churches hold to exclusive psalmody, singing only the inspired Psalms, understanding psalms, hymns and songs as three names for the Psalms. Others sing a wide range of songs. Verdict: The Psalms should have a central place in Christian worship. But the three terms most naturally describe a variety of songs, and the New Testament itself includes early Christian hymns (1:15–20; Philippians 2:6–11). Churches may sing songs that are faithful to Scripture and centred on Christ. The test is whether the word of Christ dwells richly in what is sung.

What it does not mean. It does not mean only gifted musicians sing. All believers sing.

In a sentence. Let the message of Christ dwell among you richly as you teach and admonish one another with all wisdom through psalms, hymns and songs from the Spirit, singing to God with gratitude in your hearts.

On a Tuesday. Sing a psalm or hymn today. Let the word of Christ fill your heart and home.

verseByVerse.quote: And whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him.

And whatever you do, in word or deed. Key words. Everything: speech and action, sacred and ordinary.

Do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus. Key words. In his name: as his representative, under his authority, for his glory, in dependence on him. All of life becomes worship (1 Corinthians 10:31).

Giving thanks to God the Father through him. Key words. Thankfulness for the fourth time. Through Christ we come to the Father.

What it does not mean. It does not mean saying “in Jesus’ name” like a magic formula. It means living as his.

In a sentence. And whatever you do, whether in word or deed, do it all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him.

For worship. Take an ordinary task today and do it consciously in the name of the Lord Jesus, with thanks.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul applies this to the household, the basic unit of ancient society. Wives are to submit to their husbands as fitting in the Lord, and husbands are to love their wives and not be harsh with them. Children are to obey their parents, which pleases the Lord, and fathers are not to provoke their children and discourage them. Slaves are to obey their earthly masters sincerely, not to win favour, but working wholeheartedly as for the Lord, from whom they will receive the inheritance; wrongdoers will be repaid without favouritism. Masters must treat their slaves justly and fairly, knowing they too have a Master in heaven.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lordship of Christ in the Household: Sacred and Ordinary

The household code illustrates one of Reformed theology’s most important convictions: there is no sacred-secular divide. The lordship of Christ claimed in the great hymn of chapter 1 arrives in chapter 3 at the level of household management, parenting, and the workplace. Abraham Kuyper’s “every square inch” is not abstract theology; it is the practical implication of “whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus” (3:17). The Christian who is an excellent spouse, a patient parent, and an honest worker is doing theology in the most concrete possible form.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Graeco-Roman household was organized around the absolute authority of the paterfamilias — husband, father, master. Over children and slaves his authority was close to absolute in law. Paul does not abolish this structure but fills it with a different spirit: love, not domination; encouragement, not provocation; justice, not exploitation. The counterpart to every command of submission is a command of love and care that was genuinely counter-cultural. Now: The application of these principles in contemporary household and work relationships continues to produce the same counter-cultural witness: the Christian employee who works with integrity “as to the Lord” even when unsupervised; the Christian employer who treats workers with justice and fairness; the Christian parent who encourages rather than exasperates. Each is a small enactment of the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: Wives, submit to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wives, submit to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord.

The household code. Paul now applies the new life to the household (3:18–4:1), as in Ephesians 5:21–6:9. Greek writers had household codes too, but Paul’s is unique: it addresses the weaker parties (wives, children, slaves) as responsible persons, and places duties on the stronger (husbands, fathers, masters), all under the lordship of Christ.

Wives, submit to your husbands. Key words. “Submit” (hypotassō, place yourself under, arrange under). A voluntary choice, not something husbands are told to enforce. To your own husbands: not to all men.

As is fitting in the Lord. Key words. Appropriate for those who belong to the Lord. The motive is Christ, not culture. And the limit is Christ: no wife must follow her husband into sin.

Where Christians differ: wives’ submission. Egalitarians argue that submission was a cultural accommodation, now outdated, or mutual only. Verdict: Paul grounds the wife’s submission in the Lord and elsewhere in creation and in Christ’s relationship with the church (Ephesians 5:22–33; 1 Corinthians 11:3, 8–9). It is permanent, not merely cultural. But it is a wife’s willing response to her husband’s loving, sacrificial leadership, not a licence for him to dominate. It never requires a wife to sin or to endure abuse. Abuse is a grave sin, and abused wives should seek safety and help from the church and authorities. Husband and wife are equal heirs of grace (1 Peter 3:7).

What it does not mean. It does not mean women are inferior, or that wives have no voice. It means a God-given order in marriage.

In a sentence. Wives, submit yourselves to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord.

On a Tuesday. Wives, find one way today to honour and support your husband’s leadership, as to the Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: Husbands, love your wives, and do not be harsh with them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Husbands, love your wives, and do not be harsh with them.

Husbands, love your wives. Key words. Love (agapaō): self-giving love, like Christ’s for the church (Ephesians 5:25). Greek household codes told husbands to rule; Paul tells them to love. A present tense: keep on loving.

And do not be harsh with them. Key words. “Harsh” (pikrainō, embittered, sharp, resentful). No bitterness, irritability or harshness. Male leadership is defined as gentle love. Harshness toward one’s wife hinders a man’s prayers (1 Peter 3:7).

What it does not mean. It does not mean love is only a feeling. It is action: serving, protecting, cherishing.

In a sentence. Husbands, love your wives and do not be harsh with them.

For worship. Husbands, ask God to make you gentle and loving like Christ. Confess any harshness to your wife.

verseByVerse.quote: Children, obey your parents in everything, for this pleases the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Children, obey your parents in everything, for this pleases the Lord.

Children, obey your parents in everything. Key words. Paul addresses children directly: they were present in the church when letters were read. “Obey” (hypakouō, listen to and obey). In everything: as a general rule, though not in sin, for obedience is in the Lord (Ephesians 6:1).

For this pleases the Lord. Key words. Literally, this is well-pleasing in the Lord. Children serve Christ by obeying their parents. The fifth commandment (Exodus 20:12).

What it does not mean. It does not mean children must obey parents who command sin. God’s authority is higher (Acts 5:29). And it does not mean adult children must obey parents in everything; they honour them.

In a sentence. Children, obey your parents in everything, for this pleases the Lord.

On a Tuesday. Children, obeying your parents is a way of pleasing Jesus. Do it cheerfully today.

verseByVerse.quote: Fathers, do not provoke your children, lest they become discouraged.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fathers, do not provoke your children, lest they become discouraged.

Fathers, do not provoke your children. Key words. “Provoke” (erethizō, irritate, exasperate, stir up). Through harshness, constant criticism, unfairness, favouritism, unreasonable demands, or neglect.

Lest they become discouraged. Key words. “Discouraged” (athymeō, lose heart, become dispirited). Children crushed by harsh fathers give up trying. Fathers are responsible for the spirit they create in the home. Encourage, do not crush.

What it does not mean. It does not mean fathers should not discipline. They should (Ephesians 6:4; Hebrews 12:7–11). It means discipline must be loving and fair.

In a sentence. Fathers, do not embitter your children, or they will become discouraged.

For worship. Fathers, ask God to make you an encourager of your children. Tell them today what you appreciate in them.

verseByVerse.quote: Bondservants, obey in everything those who are your earthly masters, not by way of eye-service, as people-pleasers, but with sincerity of heart, fearing the Lord. Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men, knowing that from the Lord you will receive the inheritance as your reward. You are serving the Lord Christ. For the wrongdoer will be paid back for the wrong he has done, and there is no partiality.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bondservants, obey in everything those who are your earthly masters, not by way of eye-service, as people-pleasers, but with sincerity of heart, fearing the Lord. Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men, knowing that from the Lord you will receive the inheritance as your reward. You are serving the Lord Christ. For the wrongdoer will be paid back for the wrong he has done, and there is no partiality.

Bondservants, obey in everything those who are your earthly masters. Key words. One of the slaves in the church was Onesimus, returning to his master Philemon with this letter (4:9; Philemon). Slaves were a large part of the early church. Paul addresses them as full members, responsible before Christ.

Not by way of eye-service, as people-pleasers. Key words. “Eye-service” (ophthalmodoulia): working only when watched. Paul may have coined the word.

But with sincerity of heart, fearing the Lord. Key words. Real masters is the Lord. Work from the heart because he sees.

Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men. Key words. “Heartily” (literally from the soul). Every job, even a slave’s, becomes service to Christ. The Reformers drew from this the dignity of all work: no calling is too lowly.

Knowing that from the Lord you will receive the inheritance as your reward. Key words. Slaves could not inherit under Roman law. But in Christ, they are heirs of God’s kingdom.

You are serving the Lord Christ. Key words. The heart of Christian work.

For the wrongdoer will be paid back for the wrong he has done, and there is no partiality. Key words. God judges justly. Slaves who do wrong will answer for it; and masters who abuse slaves will too (4:1). No one escapes God’s justice by status.

What it does not mean. It does not mean slavery is good. Paul elsewhere urges slaves to gain freedom if possible (1 Corinthians 7:21), condemns slave-trading (1 Timothy 1:10), and asks Philemon to receive Onesimus as a brother. It means that within the situation, believers serve Christ.

In a sentence. Slaves, obey your earthly masters in everything; and do it, not only when their eye is on you and to curry their favour, but with sincerity of heart and reverence for the Lord. Whatever you do, work at it with all your heart, as working for the Lord, not for human masters, since you know that you will receive an inheritance from the Lord as a reward. It is the Lord Christ you are serving. Anyone who does wrong will be repaid for their wrongs, and there is no favouritism.

On a Tuesday. At work today, remember: you are serving the Lord Christ. Work heartily, as for him.
verseByVerse.note: One of the slaves in the church was Onesimus, returning to his master in Colossae with this letter.
