4.title: Devoted to Prayer: Wisdom, Words, and the Gospel Network
4.overview:
The household code ends with a word to masters: treat your slaves justly and fairly, because you have a Master in heaven. Then Paul turns outward. Keep praying, alert and thankful, and pray for him: not that his prison door would open, but a door for the gospel, and that he would speak it clearly. Live wisely towards outsiders, seizing every opportunity, with speech that is gracious and seasoned with salt.

The letter closes with a page of names that shows the gospel in human form: Tychicus the courier, Onesimus the runaway slave now called a faithful brother, Mark the restored deserter, Epaphras wrestling in prayer, Luke the doctor, Demas who would later leave, Nympha and the church in her house, and Archippus, charged to finish his ministry. Paul signs with his chained hand: “Remember my chains. Grace be with you.”

verseByVerse.quote: Masters, treat your bondservants justly and fairly, knowing that you also have a Master in heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Masters, treat your bondservants justly and fairly, knowing that you also have a Master in heaven.

Meaning first. Colossians 4 finishes the household code and closes the letter. First, masters must treat their slaves justly and fairly, remembering they have a Master in heaven (v. 1). Then Paul gives three final exhortations: devote yourselves to watchful, thankful prayer, and pray for Paul’s gospel ministry; walk wisely toward outsiders, making the most of every opportunity; and let your speech be gracious and seasoned with salt (vv. 2–6). Finally, he sends news and greetings through a remarkable list of people: Tychicus the letter-carrier; Onesimus, the runaway slave now a faithful brother; fellow prisoner Aristarchus; Mark, once a deserter, now restored; Epaphras, who wrestles in prayer for them; Luke the doctor; Demas; Nympha and the church in her house; and Archippus, charged to fulfil his ministry. Paul signs with his own hand: remember my chains; grace be with you (vv. 7–18). The letter that exalted Christ over the universe ends in a network of ordinary believers bound together by him.

Masters, treat your bondservants justly and fairly. Key words. “Justly” (dikaios, what is right). “Fairly” (isotēs, equitably, literally equality). Under Roman law, slaves had almost no rights, and masters could do as they liked. Paul says masters owe slaves justice and fairness, a radical idea. The word equality hints that slaves and masters stand on the same level before God.

Knowing that you also have a Master in heaven. Key words. The same word, kyrios, lord or master. Masters are themselves slaves of Christ, and will answer to him for how they treated their slaves (Ephesians 6:9). No partiality with God (3:25).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul approved of slavery as an institution. He set principles that would undermine it: equal dignity, accountability to Christ, and brotherhood in the church (Philemon 16). Today the principle applies to employers and anyone with authority over others.

In a sentence. Masters, provide your slaves with what is right and fair, because you know that you also have a Master in heaven.

On a Tuesday. If you manage or employ others, treat them justly and fairly. You will answer to your Master in heaven.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: They are to keep on praying, alert and thankful, and to pray for Paul too, that God will open a door for the message of Christ, for which he is in chains, and that he will make it clear as he should. They should act wisely towards outsiders, making the most of every opportunity, and their conversation should always be gracious and well seasoned, so that they know how to answer each person.
verseByVerse.theology:
Prayer as Steadfast Engagement, Not Occasional Request

Paul’s instruction to “continue steadfastly in prayer” (proskartereite) reflects the Reformed conviction that prayer is not an emergency resort but the fundamental posture of the creature before the Creator. The same verb is used in Acts 1:14 of the disciples’ prayer in the upper room and in Acts 2:42 of the early church’s corporate life. Steadfast prayer is the mark of a community that has genuinely reckoned with its dependence on God and genuinely believes that prayer moves the hands that move the world.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul, in prison, could not personally open the doors for the gospel’s advance. He could pray — and he could enlist the Colossians to pray with him. The prayer for open doors is the prayer of the person who has surrendered control of the gospel’s advance to the one who actually controls it. Now: The church that wants to reach the lost but neglects corporate prayer has misunderstood the mechanism by which God works. Open doors are God’s to give; prayer is the community’s engagement with the God who gives them.

verseByVerse.quote: Continue steadfastly in prayer, being watchful in it with thanksgiving.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Continue steadfastly in prayer, being watchful in it with thanksgiving.

Continue steadfastly in prayer. Key words. “Continue steadfastly” (proskartereō, persist, devote yourselves, keep at it). The word used of the early church devoted to prayer (Acts 1:14; 2:42). Prayer is not occasional but a steady devotion.

Being watchful in it. Key words. “Watchful” (grēgoreō, stay awake, alert). Do not fall asleep in prayer, as the disciples did in Gethsemane (Mark 14:38). Stay alert to needs, temptations and Christ’s return.

With thanksgiving. Key words. Thankfulness again, the fifth time in the letter. Prayer without thanksgiving becomes complaint.

What it does not mean. It does not mean praying every second. It means a life marked by persistent, alert, grateful prayer.

In a sentence. Devote yourselves to prayer, being watchful and thankful.

For worship. Set a regular time for prayer today. Stay alert, and begin with thanks.

verseByVerse.quote: At the same time, pray also for us, that God may open to us a door for the word, to declare the mystery of Christ, on account of which I am in prison— that I may make it clear, which is how I ought to speak.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the same time, pray also for us, that God may open to us a door for the word, to declare the mystery of Christ, on account of which I am in prison—that I may make it clear, which is how I ought to speak.

At the same time, pray also for us. Key words. The great apostle asks for prayer from a small church he has never visited.

That God may open to us a door for the word. Key words. Not release from prison, but opportunity to preach. God opens doors (1 Corinthians 16:9; Acts 14:27; Revelation 3:8).

To declare the mystery of Christ, on account of which I am in prison. Key words. The mystery: Christ, including Gentiles in God’s people (1:26–27). Paul is in chains precisely because he preached it.

That I may make it clear, which is how I ought to speak. Key words. “Make clear” (phaneroō, reveal, make plain). He asks for clarity. Even Paul needed prayer to speak the gospel clearly.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul did not care about release. He cared more about the gospel.

In a sentence. And pray for us, too, that God may open a door for our message, so that we may proclaim the mystery of Christ, for which Paul is in chains. Pray that he may proclaim it clearly, as he should.

On a Tuesday. Pray for open doors and clear words for missionaries and pastors. And for yourself.

verseByVerse.quote: Walk in wisdom toward outsiders, making the best use of the time.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Walk in wisdom toward outsiders, making the best use of the time.

Walk in wisdom toward outsiders. Key words. Outsiders: unbelievers. Live wisely before them, so that your conduct commends the gospel (1 Thessalonians 4:12; 1 Peter 2:12).

Making the best use of the time. Key words. Literally, buying up the opportunity (exagorazomai ton kairon), as a merchant snaps up a bargain. Every encounter with an unbeliever is an opportunity. Seize it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean being pushy or manipulative. It means being wise, alert and ready.

In a sentence. Be wise in the way you act toward outsiders; make the most of every opportunity.

For worship. Ask God to show you one opportunity today to speak or act for Christ with an unbeliever.

verseByVerse.quote: Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how you ought to answer each person.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how you ought to answer each person.

Let your speech always be gracious. Key words. Literally, with grace: kind, attractive, pleasant. Not harsh, sarcastic or preachy.

Seasoned with salt. Key words. Salt gives flavour and preserves. Speech that is interesting, wise and wholesome, not bland or corrupt. Greek writers used salt for wit.

So that you may know how you ought to answer each person. Key words. Each person is different. Fitting answers for each (1 Peter 3:15). Wisdom listens before speaking.

What it does not mean. It does not mean compromising truth to be pleasant. It means speaking truth graciously.

In a sentence. Let your conversation be always full of grace, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how to answer everyone.

On a Tuesday. Before you speak today, ask: is this gracious? Is it seasoned with salt?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul closes with news and greetings that show the network of people behind his mission. Tychicus will bring the letter and his news, together with Onesimus, the runaway slave now a faithful brother. Aristarchus, Mark (Barnabas’s cousin), and Jesus called Justus send greetings, the only Jewish believers working with him, and a comfort to him. Epaphras, their own founder, wrestles in prayer for them and for Laodicea and Hierapolis. Luke the doctor and Demas greet them. Paul asks them to greet the church in Nympha’s house, to exchange letters with Laodicea, and to tell Archippus to complete his ministry. He signs the greeting in his own hand: remember my chains; grace be with you.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Community of the Gospel as the Body of Christ

The list of names at the end of Colossians is the practical expression of the ecclesiology of 1:18: Christ is the head of the body, the church. The body is not an abstract entity; it is Tychicus and Onesimus and Luke and Nympha. The community of grace is always concrete, always named, always embodied in particular people with particular histories, gifts, and needs. Reformed ecclesiology has always insisted on the visible, particular, local church as the primary form of the body of Christ: not an ideal church somewhere, but this church, these people, this place, this time.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Onesimus is the most striking name on the list. The runaway slave, the subject of the letter to Philemon, is now a “faithful and beloved brother” being commended to the Colossians. The gospel has done exactly what Paul said it would do in 3:11: it has abolished the slave/free distinction as a defining category. Onesimus and Philemon are brothers; Onesimus and the Colossians are family. Now: The community of the gospel is always the community of the surprising, the reconciled, the transformed. The people who would never have been in the same room together are gathered at the same table because Christ is all, and in all.

verseByVerse.quote: Tychicus will tell you all about my activities. He is a beloved brother and faithful minister and fellow servant in the Lord. I have sent him to you for this very purpose, that you may know how we are and that he may encourage your hearts,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tychicus will tell you all about my activities. He is a beloved brother and faithful minister and fellow servant in the Lord. I have sent him to you for this very purpose, that you may know how we are and that he may encourage your hearts,

Tychicus will tell you all about my activities. Key words. Tychicus, from the province of Asia, travelled with Paul (Acts 20:4) and carried this letter, Ephesians and probably Philemon (Ephesians 6:21–22). He would give news in person.

He is a beloved brother and faithful minister and fellow servant in the Lord. Key words. Three titles: family, faithful service, partnership.

I have sent him to you for this very purpose, that you may know how we are and that he may encourage your hearts. Key words. News and encouragement. Christian fellowship includes sharing news and strengthening one another.

What it does not mean. It does not mean only famous Christians matter. Tychicus was a faithful letter carrier, and Scripture honours him.

In a sentence. Tychicus will tell you all the news about Paul. He is a dear brother, a faithful minister and fellow servant in the Lord. Paul is sending him to you for the express purpose that you may know about our circumstances and that he may encourage your hearts.

For worship. Thank God for faithful, behind-the-scenes servants like Tychicus.

verseByVerse.quote: and with him Onesimus, our faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you. They will tell you of everything that has taken place here.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and with him Onesimus, our faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you. They will tell you of everything that has taken place here.

And with him Onesimus. Key words. Onesimus was the runaway slave of Philemon, a member of the Colossian church. He had met Paul in prison and been converted (Philemon 10). Now he returns to his master with Paul’s letter to Philemon.

Our faithful and beloved brother. Key words. Not “the runaway slave,” but faithful and beloved brother. Paul honours him with the same words used of Tychicus.

Who is one of you. Key words. He belongs to Colossae, and now belongs to the church there.

They will tell you of everything that has taken place here. Key words. Onesimus, a slave, is trusted as a messenger alongside Tychicus. The gospel transforms status.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul excused Onesimus’s wrong. Philemon shows that he sought reconciliation and restitution. But grace made him a brother.

In a sentence. He is coming with Onesimus, our faithful and dear brother, who is one of you. They will tell you everything that is happening here.

On a Tuesday. No one is beyond God’s grace. Welcome converts with a past as faithful and beloved brothers and sisters.
verseByVerse.note: Onesimus was the runaway slave of Philemon, a member of the church at Colossae.

verseByVerse.quote: Aristarchus my fellow prisoner greets you, and Mark the cousin of Barnabas (concerning whom you have received instructions—if he comes to you, welcome him), and Jesus who is called Justus. These are the only men of the circumcision among my fellow workers for the kingdom of God, and they have been a comfort to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Aristarchus my fellow prisoner greets you, and Mark the cousin of Barnabas (concerning whom you have received instructions—if he comes to you, welcome him), and Jesus who is called Justus. These are the only men of the circumcision among my fellow workers for the kingdom of God, and they have been a comfort to me.

Aristarchus my fellow prisoner greets you. Key words. A Macedonian from Thessalonica, seized in the Ephesian riot, and Paul’s companion on the voyage to Rome (Acts 19:29; 27:2). Perhaps he voluntarily shared Paul’s imprisonment.

And Mark the cousin of Barnabas. Key words. Mark had once left Paul, causing a split with Barnabas; he is now restored and useful (Acts 13:13; 15:37–39; 2 Timothy 4:11). A beautiful picture of reconciliation. Later he wrote the Gospel of Mark.

(Concerning whom you have received instructions—if he comes to you, welcome him). Key words. Some churches may have been wary of Mark because of his past. Paul says: welcome him.

And Jesus who is called Justus. Key words. Jesus (Joshua) was a common Jewish name. Otherwise unknown.

These are the only men of the circumcision among my fellow workers for the kingdom of God. Key words. Only three Jewish Christians were working with Paul at this point. Many Jewish believers opposed him.

And they have been a comfort to me. Key words. “Comfort” (parēgoria, soothing, from which paregoric, a medicine). They were medicine to his soul.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Mark’s earlier failure did not matter. It means failure need not be final.

In a sentence. Paul’s fellow prisoner Aristarchus sends you his greetings, as does Mark, the cousin of Barnabas. (You have received instructions about him; if he comes to you, welcome him.) Jesus, who is called Justus, also sends greetings. These are the only Jews among Paul’s co-workers for the kingdom of God, and they have proved a comfort to him.

For worship. If you have failed in serving God, take heart from Mark. God restores. And be a comfort to those who serve.
verseByVerse.note: Mark had once left Paul, causing a split with Barnabas; he is now restored.

verseByVerse.quote: Epaphras, who is one of you, a servant of Christ Jesus, greets you, always struggling on your behalf in his prayers, that you may stand mature and fully assured in all the will of God. For I bear him witness that he has worked hard for you and for those in Laodicea and in Hierapolis.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Epaphras, who is one of you, a servant of Christ Jesus, greets you, always struggling on your behalf in his prayers, that you may stand mature and fully assured in all the will of God. For I bear him witness that he has worked hard for you and for those in Laodicea and in Hierapolis.

Epaphras, who is one of you, a servant of Christ Jesus, greets you. Key words. The founder of the church (1:7). “Servant” (doulos, slave), a title Paul uses for himself.

Always struggling on your behalf in his prayers. Key words. “Struggling” (agōnizomai, wrestling, agonising, the word Paul used of himself in 1:29; 2:1). Prayer as hard labour, like an athlete straining. Epaphras could not be with them, but fought for them in prayer.

That you may stand mature and fully assured in all the will of God. Key words. His prayer: maturity (teleioi) and full assurance (peplērophorēmenoi, fully convinced). Not swayed by false teaching.

For I bear him witness that he has worked hard for you and for those in Laodicea and in Hierapolis. Key words. Hierapolis lay across the valley from Laodicea, about six miles away, famous for hot springs. Epaphras cared for all three churches.

What it does not mean. It does not mean prayer is only for spiritual giants. Every believer can wrestle in prayer.

In a sentence. Epaphras, who is one of you and a servant of Christ Jesus, sends greetings. He is always wrestling in prayer for you, that you may stand firm in all the will of God, mature and fully assured. Paul vouches for him that he is working hard for you and for those at Laodicea and Hierapolis.

On a Tuesday. Wrestle in prayer for your church today, like Epaphras.
verseByVerse.note: Hierapolis lay across the valley from Laodicea.

verseByVerse.quote: Luke the beloved physician greets you, as does Demas.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke the beloved physician greets you, as does Demas.

Luke the beloved physician greets you. Key words. Luke, the author of Luke and Acts, was a doctor, probably a Gentile (he is not among the men of the circumcision, v. 11). He travelled with Paul and stayed with him to the end (2 Timothy 4:11). Beloved: Paul’s dear friend, and perhaps his doctor.

As does Demas. Key words. Demas later deserted Paul, “in love with this present world” (2 Timothy 4:10). Here he is still a fellow worker (Philemon 24). Notice: no warm words for Demas, perhaps a hint. A sober warning that serving alongside great Christians does not guarantee faithfulness to the end.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Demas was certainly lost. Scripture does not tell us his end. It means we must guard our hearts against love of the world.

In a sentence. Our dear friend Luke, the doctor, and Demas send greetings.

For worship. Ask God to keep you faithful to the end, and not let love of the world draw you away.
verseByVerse.note: Luke, the author of Luke and Acts, was a doctor. Demas later deserted Paul.

verseByVerse.quote: Give my greetings to the brothers at Laodicea, and to Nympha and the church in her house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Give my greetings to the brothers at Laodicea, and to Nympha and the church in her house.

Give my greetings to the brothers at Laodicea. Key words. The neighbouring church (2:1).

And to Nympha and the church in her house. Key words. Churches met in homes, often hosted by wealthier believers. Nympha was a woman who hosted a church, perhaps in Laodicea. Some manuscripts read a man’s name, Nymphas, and “his house,” as the ESV note mentions; the feminine reading is better supported.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Nympha was the pastor. Hosting a church was a valuable ministry of hospitality.

In a sentence. Give Paul’s greetings to the brothers and sisters at Laodicea, and to Nympha and the church in her house.

On a Tuesday. Could your home be used for church life: a Bible study, prayer meeting, or hospitality?
verseByVerse.note: Churches met in homes.

verseByVerse.quote: And when this letter has been read among you, have it also read in the church of the Laodiceans; and see that you also read the letter from Laodicea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when this letter has been read among you, have it also read in the church of the Laodiceans; and see that you also read the letter from Laodicea.

And when this letter has been read among you. Key words. Letters were read aloud in church gatherings, as Scripture (1 Thessalonians 5:27).

Have it also read in the church of the Laodiceans. Key words. Apostolic letters were shared between churches. This was the beginning of the collection of the New Testament.

And see that you also read the letter from Laodicea. Key words. The letter from Laodicea has not survived; some think it may be our Ephesians, which may have been a circular letter to several churches (some early manuscripts lack “in Ephesus” in Ephesians 1:1). A forged “Epistle to the Laodiceans” appeared later, but was rejected.

Where Christians differ: lost letters and the canon. If an apostolic letter is lost, is the New Testament incomplete? Verdict: God in his providence preserved the books he intended for the permanent canon. Not every apostolic letter was meant to be Scripture for all time; or, if the letter from Laodicea is Ephesians, it was not lost at all. The canon is complete and sufficient (Westminster 1.2–3, 6).

What it does not mean. It does not mean the church created Scripture. The church recognised the Scriptures God gave.

In a sentence. After this letter has been read to you, see that it is also read in the church of the Laodiceans and that you in turn read the letter from Laodicea.

For worship. Thank God for preserving his word for you. Read it aloud with others.
verseByVerse.note: The letter from Laodicea has not survived; some think it may be the letter we know as Ephesians.

verseByVerse.quote: And say to Archippus, “See that you fulfill the ministry that you have received in the Lord.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
And say to Archippus, “See that you fulfill the ministry that you have received in the Lord.”

And say to Archippus. Key words. Archippus was probably a member of Philemon’s household, perhaps his son (Philemon 2), and seems to have had a ministry in the church, perhaps leading it while Epaphras was away.

“See that you fulfill the ministry that you have received in the Lord.” Key words. A public charge, read before the church. “Fulfil” (plēroō, complete). Perhaps he was discouraged, or neglecting his task. The ministry was received in the Lord: given by Christ, and to be completed for him (2 Timothy 4:5).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Archippus was in serious sin. It means he needed encouragement to persevere.

In a sentence. Tell Archippus: “See to it that you complete the ministry you have received in the Lord.”

On a Tuesday. What ministry have you received from the Lord? Fulfil it. Do not give up.
verseByVerse.note: Archippus was probably a member of Philemon’s household.

verseByVerse.quote: I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand. Remember my chains. Grace be with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand. Remember my chains. Grace be with you.

I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand. Key words. Paul dictated his letters, then signed the greeting himself, as a mark of authenticity (2 Thessalonians 3:17).

Remember my chains. Key words. Perhaps the chain was clanking as he wrote. Remember me in prayer, and remember what the gospel costs (Hebrews 13:3).

Grace be with you. Key words. The shortest of Paul’s closings. Everything Christ has done for us is grace. Some manuscripts add Amen.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul was seeking pity. He was seeking prayer and solidarity.

In a sentence. Paul writes this greeting in his own hand. Remember his chains. Grace be with you.

For worship. Remember the chains of persecuted believers today. Pray for them, and thank God for his grace.
verseByVerse.note: Paul dictated his letters, then signed the greeting himself.
